messages.body_plain:
This message is relevant for users of Distance for Windows who make use
of the analysis engines that call R - that is the MRDS, DSM and MA
analysis engines.

In the most recent release of R, that is version 4.2, the R for Windows
build has stopped supporting 32-bit R.  This is the version called by
Distance for Windows.  Hence, at present Distance for Windows is not
compatible with the latest version of R.  We therefore suggest users do
not upgrade beyond R 4.1.2, which is the version supported by our
current release of Distance for Windows (version 7.4 Release 2).  If
users do wish to upgrade their version of R, they should retain version
4.1.2 on their computer so that Distance for Windows can still call it
to run the analysis engines.

We are planning a new release of Distance for Windows for the end of
July (version 7.5 Release 1) that will fix this issue.

Best wishes, Len Thomas

messages.subject_clean: post-stratification by object where there are geographic strata?
messages.body_plain:
Good day,

We analyzed DS data from a line-transect survey with 2 geographic strata (high and low density). The high-density stratum was sampled more intensively.

We would like to post-stratify by age-sex class to estimate numbers and proportions of adult males, adult females, and "other" (younger) bears across the entire study area. However, the documentation specifies that only one type of stratification is supported by dht2, and when I attempt to retain information about the geographic strata when post-stratifying by age-sex class (stratifying by "object"), I get errors such as:
">1 Area defined for a single stratum label, check data", OR,
"Only one level of stratification is currently supported"

When I remove information about the geographic strata, I can post-stratify by age-sex class, but the estimated total density and abundance are quite different (higher) than those from the geographically stratified analysis. It seems inappropriate to present numbers or proportions of animals in different age-sex classes estimated while ignoring the geographic strata in this situation, especially because the age-sex distribution of animals likely varies by strata (higher proportion of adult males in the high density stratum).

Is there a simple solution to this problem? I doubt that we have sufficient detections in the low-density stratum to analyze the data from the 2 geographic strata separately.

Thanks for your attention,
Eric

messages.subject_clean: Full likelihood approach: the likelihood component pertaining to the detection model with continuous coviarates & handling nested covariates
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

We've been working on Oedekoven (2020)'s code <https://examples.distancesampling.org/book-bobwhite/bobwhite.htm> for a full likelihood approach to fit a half-normal detection function to line transect data. For our detection model we're using the continous covariates of forbs height (F_HT_MDN) and cover (F_CVR_MDN) median values per transect, whereas for our count model we're using the continous covariates of plot age (OP_AGE) and Julian date (JDctr). However, I've a couple of questions regading the ml.log.lik function:
In part 2, how do I handle continous covariates as opposed to factorial covariates (as shown in the example <https://examples.distancesampling.org/book-bobwhite/bobwhite.html#defining-the-likelihood-function-for-the-maximum-likelihood-approach>)? Also, how do I handle more than one covariate here?
Here's the code adapted to our data:
  # Part 2
  # the likelihood component pertaining to the detection model
  # calculating the f(y) for each observed distances
  le<-nrow(datax$dis.object)
  fe<-numeric(le)
  allf.ht <http://allf.ht><-sort(unique(datax$dis.object$F_HT_MDN))
  dis.f.ht <http://dis.f.ht><-match(datax$dis.object$F_HT_MDN,allf.ht <http://allf.ht>)
  allf.cvr<-sort(unique(datax$dis.object$F_CVR_MDN))
  dis.f.cvr<-match(datax$dis.object$F_CVR_MDN,allf.cvr)
  # the sigma(z) for each detection
  allscale<-exp(scale.int <http://scale.int>+sig.f.ht <http://sig.f.ht>[dis.f.ht <http://dis.f.ht>]+sig.f.cvr[dis.f.cvr])
The issue appears to be in the allscale line, where everything shows as NA. I reckon this is due to the handling of continous as opposed to categorical data.
Right now we're using OP_AGE as a continous covariate (0 to 18, where 0 represents active plots, and 18 correspond to unmodified habitat, whereas all inbetween are fallow lands of varous ages since abandonment), but we're interested in implementing a nested design where a continous covariate (age) is nested inside a factor covariate. Is this possible?
Thanks in advance for the help.

Hi Elipaleth,

Great you are using the code and sorry to hear you had trouble making it work for your own study.

In general, using a continuous covariate should be easier than a factor covariate and you can simply set up multiple continuous, multiple factor or a combination of both.

Here is an example of how you would set up the scale for two continuous covariates. Remember you might have to force R to look at your variable as a numeric variable by using e.g. as.numeric(datax$dis.object$F_HT_MDN).

# you don’t need these lines anymore

#allf.ht <http://allf.ht><-sort(unique(datax$dis.object$F_HT_MDN))

#  dis.f.ht <http://dis.f.ht><-match(datax$dis.object$F_HT_MDN,allf.ht <http://allf.ht>)

#  allf.cvr<-sort(unique(datax$dis.object$F_CVR_MDN))

#  dis.f.cvr<-match(datax$dis.object$F_CVR_MDN,allf.cvr)

   # the sigma(z) for each detection

  allscale<-exp(scale.int <http://scale.int>+sig.f.ht <http://sig.f.ht>*datax$dis.object$F_HT_MDN )+sig.f.cvr*datax$dis.object$F_CVR_MDN

Now, sig.f.ht <http://sig.f.ht> and sig.f.cvr are each a single coefficient associated with their respective variables.

I am not sure I follow your second question. Do you mean that age might have a different effect depending on the type of habitat? If that is the case, here is an example of how you might set this up. Let’s say habitat is a factor covariate and age is a continuous covariate. You could use an interaction term in the model. This will give you different slope coefficients for age for each habitat (in addition to the coefficients for each habitat). If you are interested in setting up such an interaction term for one of your models, it gets a bit complicated but I can try to help you work this out if you wish.

Hope this helps. Cheers, Cornelia

messages.body_plain:
Hello Distance Team,

I'm using a cluster analysis for transect distance surveys of a low population density of Gopher Tortoises. I'm using a modified method (following Stober et al. 2017 but without the stratified estimator) in which the search object is Gopher Tortoise burrows and burrow occupancy is coded as group size. (occupied=1, unoccupied=0, unknown=-1). In Distance for windows, I achieved this with the option, "use mean of observed clusters". It was my understanding that the analysis considers all the burrows detected (n=103) and uses burrow occupancy (mean of cluster size) to estimate density and abundance of tortoises (rather than burrows). The idea is to increase the sample size to achieve a lower CV. I'm migrating my analysis to the R packages, and it seems that ds is ignoring the burrows with group size of 0. So instead of having a sample size of 103, I have a sample size of 19. Is there a way to replicate the windows analysis in R that still uses all burrows while accounting for occupancy?

Best,
Kammie

Kammie

You are right that assigning group size of 0 is not recognised by the ds​ function of the Distance package to do what you want.

You will need to compute to occupancy proportion (and its standard error) outside of the ds​ function, then use dht2​ to pass along this multiplier and its uncertainty into the computation of tortoise density.

>From your note, it seems occupancy is 19/103=0.184.  The standard error of this occupancy estimate is calculated using

sqrt((p*(1-p))/n)

which I make to be 0.0382 (check my arithmetic).

Look at the example of an analysis of dung on our examples page to see how to create a multiplier object and add that object as a multiplier​ argument to the dht2​ function to convert your estimate of burrow density into an estimate of occupied burrow density:
http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-mult/multipliers-distill.html
Multipliers and indirect surveys - Distance Sampling <http://examples.distancesampling.org/Distance-mult/multipliers-distill.html>
The final step is to use these multipliers to convert \(\hat D_{\textrm{pellet groups}}\) to \(\hat D_{\textrm{deer}}\) (as in the equations above) - for this we need to employ the dht2 function. messages.body_plain:
We are in a bit of a pickle regarding how (and whether) we
should apply the distance sampling framework on our drone imagery strip
transects.  Is there a procedure within the distance sampling framework
that can deal with detection not being 100 % inside a strip transect? Classic
strip transects assume that all objects are detected in the covered area, which
is far from the case with counts from our drone images. Analyzing the data in a
‘distance sampling’ framework with a uniform key function (no detection
covariates allowed) is not ideal since detection is still not perfect due to
background, image quality and solar angle (creating shadows) and such. We had
seven independent observers going through the same imagery and observer
detection of the “true” animals was in average 75 % (but varies depending on
the covariates). The drone imagery is captured from a constant altitude so
distance away from observer is the same on all imagery and thus distance from
observer to animal does not influence detection.

The second alternative is to use a hurdle density surface
model to get the abundance. We have been looking at the dshm_fit with ds()
integrated but are running into the same problem. This function uses the same
ds() function from the Distance package, thus would force us back to use
uniform key function without covariates following the assumption of no
detection error. How to integrate differences in detection probability between
observers (for both P/A and count models) and possibly other covariates (e.g.,
image quality)?

So.. what is the best way to integrate detection in a density surface model when the drone strip transect violates distance sampling assumptions? Hoping for some useful suggestions as we are currently spinning our wheels a bit!

You are correct that multispecies surveys, particularly with additional stratification can present problems when subsetting data.  This can be caused by the subsetting resulting in aspects of the study design not being respected. Hi Ingrid, hi listfolks,

I've spent a bit of time working on this but we've not finished that
particular analysis. So, I'm not sure if what I say below would equate
to anything like "the best way" to do it.

One way to approach this is to see the problem as not a distance
sampling one... in a DSM the detection function models the observation
process, then the GAM will deal with spatial effects. You can think of
your verification of the images as a kind of observation process in
itself, that you switch-out for the usual distance sampling model.

For example, in our case we had a mark-recapture observation process and
used the probability of capture in our DSM, then were able to propagate
uncertainty through the model for that. This required a fair amount of
custom coding to get things to work but it is doable.

If your observation process didn't depend on covariates, things would be
slightly easier as you'd simple be able to use your (say) 0.75 as an
offset in the model (the easiest way is to use the availability=...
argument) and fit things that way, then you can include uncertainty by
adding squared CVs, but if covariates are involved then adding the
squared CVs will leave out covariance between the observation and
spatial models (as it assumes independence between the processes). That
being said, that's probably not a bad starting point, then you can
consider fleshing the model out with a more complex observation process
model.

Hope that helps,
--dave

messages.body_plain:
Eudald

Thanks for sending along all the components of your distance sampling data.  The problem that you detected arose because your perpendicular distances appear in disdata​ and in that file you have those distances associated with sequential values (1, 2, 3, ..., 48) in the field X​.  In obs_table​ you had the field object​ that contained values up to 66, with 18 values missing (resulting in 48 records in the file).  When the software tried to find distances for objects​ numbered > 48, it could find none.  The objects numbered > 48 all fell into the strata Forques and Pleta; hence the function had no distances to assign to those strata.

There needs to be a connection between the information in disdata​ and obs_table​.  The way I made this happen was to replace the object​ values in obs_table​ with the sequential values in the field X​.  You can see what I did in the following code:

library(Distance)
setwd("E:/troubleshoot/Eudald")
disdata <- read.csv("distance_data.csv")
obs_table <- read.csv("obs_table.csv")
region_table <- read.csv("region_table.csv")
region_table$Area <- region_table$Area / 10000 # convert to hectares
sample_table <- read.csv("sample_table.csv")
# re-define the Obs table field "object" to point to the sequential numbers
obs_table$object <- NULL
obs_table$object <- obs_table$X
# make a unit conversion so density is per hectare
convunit <- convert_units("meter", "meter", "hectare")
out <- ds(data=disdata,

   obs_table = obs_table,
   sample_table = sample_table,
   region_table = region_table,

   transect = "line",
   convert_units = convunit)
summary(out)

Note that I also made some adjustments to the Area units such that the output would produce density estimates in lizards per hectare rather than lizards per sq. meter.
